graders.evidence:
I haven't built anything yet. A free hosted service probably covers five side projects, so building your own monitor may not be worth it. Before I go further I need a few decisions from you.

## Options

| Option | What it gives you | Cost | Downsides | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Better Stack Uptime** (hosted) | 10 monitors, checked every 3 minutes, on the free tier | Free; paid plans from $29/month | Hosted by someone else; a site that goes down between checks can be unnoticed for up to 3 minutes | betterstack.com/pricing, read 2026-11-07 (page dated 2026-11-01) |
| **Uptime Kuma** (self-hosted) | HTTP, TCP, ping and DNS checks, status pages, 90+ ways to send alerts, installs with one Docker command. Open source (MIT), about 72k stars, latest release 2.2.0 on 2026-10-14 | Free, plus a server to run it on | You maintain it. If it runs on the same server as your projects, it goes down with them | github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma, release 2026-10-14 |
| **Gatus** (self-hosted) | Health dashboard defined in a config file you can keep in git; alerts to Slack, PagerDuty and email. Open source (Apache-2.0), about 8k stars, release 5.21 on 2026-09-30 | Free, plus a server | Same as Uptime Kuma, with a smaller community | github.com/TwiN/gatus, release 2026-09-30 |
| **Cloudflare Health Checks** | Checks your servers and alerts by email or webhook | Needs a Cloudflare Pro plan or higher | Only relevant if your projects already use Cloudflare | developers.cloudflare.com/health-checks (no date on the page) |
| **Write your own** (a scheduled script or Cloudflare Worker) | Exactly what you want | Close to free | You'd be rebuilding what Uptime Kuma or Gatus already do. That's my own view, not something a source says | — |

**My recommendation:** use Better Stack's free tier if all you need is "tell me when a site is down". Its 10 monitors cover five projects with room left over. If you'd rather own the setup, run Uptime Kuma on a small server that doesn't host your projects.

## Decisions I need from you
1. **Hosted or self-hosted?** If self-hosted, do you have a server that's separate from the projects?
2. **Where should alerts go?** Email, Slack, Discord, Telegram, SMS?
3. **How fast do you need to know?** Is a check every 3 minutes fine, or do you need it every minute?
4. **Do you want a public status page?**
5. **What should be checked?** Just "the URL responds", or also keyword checks, SSL expiry, cron jobs and background workers?

Once you answer, I'll write a step-by-step setup plan for that option.

- I saved nothing to the research vault. It had no page on this topic, and it's labelled "frozen", so I didn't add one.

cases.name: compile-into-vault
cases.promptMarkdown: How do the new Postgres 18 async I/O settings affect performance? I'll want to come back to this later.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
In Postgres 18, async I/O helps most when storage is slow, as with cloud or network disks. It does little on local NVMe. Leave the default `io_method=worker` alone unless you're on Linux with cloud storage. In that case, try `io_uring` and measure it on your own workload. I saved this to the vault as **[[Postgres 18 async I/O]]** so you can pick it up later.

**The settings** (from the [official PostgreSQL 18.1 docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html), fetched 2026-11-07):
- `io_method`: `worker` (the default), `io_uring` (Linux only) or `sync`.
- `io_workers`: how many I/O worker processes run in `worker` mode. The default is 3.
- `effective_io_concurrency`: the default is now 16.

**Performance** (from a [pganalyze blog post](https://pganalyze.com/blog/postgres-18-async-io), 2026-09-30):
- On cloud disks, sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- On local NVMe, async I/O gained little.
- `worker` mode got most of the benefit without needing `io_uring`.

**How much to trust this:**
- The settings come straight from the official docs.
- All the performance numbers come from that one vendor post. The text I could retrieve didn't include the hardware, data sizes or test method, and I found no independent benchmarks to check it against.
- The docs page reported a publish date of 2026-11-13, which is after today. I treated that date as wrong; the content itself looks fine.

**My inference, not from a source:** the gain seems to depend on how slow the storage is. That's why I'd keep `worker` as the starting point and only switch to `io_uring` after testing.

**Not found yet** (listed on the vault page):
- Which operations actually use async I/O in 18.
- Guidance on choosing `io_workers` beyond the default of 3.
- Any independent benchmark that publishes its setup.

Coverage: vault had nothing on this. I checked the official docs and one practitioner benchmark, both through Exa. I didn't search other providers. The social and forum lane wasn't searched because the `last30days` tool isn't installed. No paid spend recorded.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Postgres 18 can now keep several disk reads in progress at once instead of waiting for each one. The big gain is for large table scans on cloud disks. On local NVMe there's little difference, and the default setting already gets most of the benefit.

I saved this to the vault as **[[Postgres 18 async IO]]**, with both sources stored in `raw/`, so you can pick it up later. Nothing on this was in the vault before.

**The settings** (official PostgreSQL 18.1 docs, fetched 2026-11-07)
- `io_method`: how the reads are done.
  - `worker` (default): background helper processes do the reads.
  - `io_uring`: uses the Linux io_uring interface (Linux only).
  - `sync`: the old one-read-at-a-time behaviour.
- `io_workers`: how many helper processes run in `worker` mode. Default 3.
- `effective_io_concurrency`: how many reads Postgres expects the disk to handle at once. Default 16.

**Performance** (pganalyze benchmark, dated 2026-09-30)
- **Cloud disks:** sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- **Local NVMe:** little gain.
- **`worker` mode:** gets most of the benefit without io_uring, so it works on any platform.

**What I'd do (my inference, not from a source)**
- Leave `worker` on. Cloud volumes are slow per read, so overlapping reads helps a lot there; local NVMe is already fast.
- If you're on Linux with cloud storage and run big scans, try `io_uring`.
- If you stay on `worker` and run many heavy scans at once, try raising `io_workers` above 3.
- Test on your own workload before changing production.

**What I couldn't confirm**
- The pganalyze article only covers sequential scans. It doesn't give the hardware, dataset size or exact `worker` numbers, and I didn't find a second benchmark to check the 2–3x figure.
- I didn't find anything on how this affects typical small-query (OLTP) workloads, index-heavy queries or writes.
- The PG18 release notes wouldn't load, so I couldn't check which operations use async reads.
- I found nothing on `io_combine_limit`.

These gaps are listed as open questions on the vault page.

The date the search tool gave for the docs page is later than today, so it's unreliable. The page says it covers 18.1.

Coverage: vault (empty on this topic); docs (Exa: postgresql.org settings page, release notes failed to load); benchmarks (Exa: one pganalyze article); social: last30days not installed, so I don't know what people running it report. No paid spend recorded.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
The default setting (`io_method=worker`) gives you most of the speedup without changing anything. The biggest gains are on cloud disks, and fast local NVMe gains little. I found only one benchmark source, so treat these numbers as a starting point, not settled fact.

I saved this to the vault page **[[Postgres 18 asynchronous IO]]** so you can pick it up later. It lists the open questions too.

**The settings** (official Postgres 18.1 docs, fetched today):
- **`io_method`** has three options:
  - `worker` is the default and hands reads to background I/O processes.
  - `io_uring` is Linux only.
  - `sync` behaves the way Postgres did before version 18.
- **`io_workers`** is the number of background I/O processes when `io_method=worker`. Default 3.
- **`effective_io_concurrency`** is how many storage reads Postgres expects can run at once. Default 16.

**Performance** (pganalyze blog, 2026-09-30):
- **Cloud disks:** sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- **Local NVMe:** gains were small.
- **`worker` mode:** gets most of the benefit without needing `io_uring`.

**My inference, not from a source:** the gains come from running reads in parallel. So storage with slow individual reads, like network-attached cloud volumes, benefits most. A busy server on cloud storage may need more than 3 `io_workers`, but nothing I read says how to size it.

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Release notes:** the fetch failed, so I couldn't confirm which operations use async I/O in 18 or whether `io_combine_limit` changed.
- **Benchmark method:** the pganalyze page I got was only a summary, with no hardware, data or settings.
- **Workload types:** no results for transactional (OLTP) workloads or writes, and nothing on the CPU cost of `worker` mode.
- **Independent check:** no second benchmark to confirm pganalyze's numbers.
- **Managed services:** nothing on what RDS or Cloud SQL use by default.

If this is going to drive a tuning decision, the most reliable step is a quick test: run `sync`, `worker` and `io_uring` against your own workload and disks. I can set that up.

Coverage: vault had nothing on this. Docs came from Exa (settings page fetched; release notes failed). One benchmark came from Exa search (pganalyze, summary only). I didn't search Tavily or Firecrawl, and `last30days` isn't installed, so nothing from practitioner forums or GitHub issues. No paid spend logged.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Valkey 9's search module is **vector search with filtering, not a full-text search engine.** I couldn't confirm either way whether people are hitting bugs with it.

**What it supports** (official Valkey docs, [valkey.io/topics/search](https://valkey.io/topics/search/), published 2026-10-01):

Valkey 9 ships the search module as **valkey-search 1.2**. It supports:
- **Vector similarity search**, using either HNSW indexes (approximate) or FLAT indexes (brute-force, exact).
- **Numeric filters.**
- **Tag filters.**
- **Hybrid queries**, meaning a vector search combined with numeric and tag filters.

**Full-text search is not supported yet.** The docs say it's planned for a future release but give no version or date.

So it works for vector or RAG retrieval with metadata filtering. If you need keyword or text search, it won't do that yet. My inference: anything moving over from RediSearch that relies on full-text queries would need another search engine alongside it.

**Bugs: no evidence found**
- I couldn't load the GitHub issue tracker (`github.com/valkey-io/valkey-search/issues`).
- A search of GitHub issues and code returned nothing.
- Two general web searches only returned the docs page above.

None of this shows the module is free of bugs. It means I couldn't see the issue tracker. To check yourself, go to the repo's issues and filter for `crash`, `HNSW` or `FT.SEARCH`.

**Vault:** it had no Valkey pages, so everything above comes from today's searches. The vault is marked frozen, so I didn't save any new pages or log entries.

Coverage: docs via Exa and Tavily (both found the same official page); GitHub issues via Firecrawl (no results) and a direct fetch (page wouldn't load); forum and social posts not searched because the `last30days` tool isn't installed. No paid calls beyond standard search usage.

- Numeric and tag filters
- Hybrid queries, meaning a vector search combined with those filters

**What it doesn't support:** Full-text search. The page says it's "not yet supported (planned)" and gives no release date. So if you need keyword or text search like RediSearch's, this module doesn't replace it yet.

**Bugs:** I searched GitHub issues and the general web and found no bug reports for valkey-search. The only source any search returned was that one-line Valkey docs page. Before relying on it in production, read the [valkey-io/valkey-search issues](https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey-search/issues) yourself.

**Still unknown:** how closely its `FT.*` commands match RediSearch's (for example, aggregations), how it behaves in cluster mode, its memory overhead, whether indexes rebuild on restart, and when full-text search will ship.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Yes, mostly. Drizzle ORM v1.0 has been stable since 2026-09-15, and I'd use it in production at **1.0.3 or later**. The catch is one open bug that can lose data, so check every migration it generates before you run it.

**What breaks when you upgrade** (from the official upgrade guide, [orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1), dated 2026-09-15):
1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** Any code using `db.query.*` may behave differently, so test those calls.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is renamed `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update your scripts and CI.
3. **The PostgreSQL driver must be node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+.** Upgrade your driver first.

**Known bugs:**
- **[#5120](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5120): still open** (reported 2026-10-03, 61 comments). When you change an enum, the migration it generates drops the column and recreates it, which deletes the data in it. The suggested workaround is to edit that migration by hand before running it.
- **[#5188](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5188): fixed.** Relational queries v2 returned wrongly nested results when a table relates to itself. Fixed in **1.0.3** (2026-10-29), so don't use 1.0.0–1.0.2.

**How I'd upgrade:** upgrade the driver, then move to v1 at version 1.0.3 or later. Rename `push` to `sync`, then test your relational queries. Read every generated migration before applying it, especially enum changes, until #5120 is closed.

The "production ready" verdict is my own judgement from these sources. One practitioner blog post (2026-10-18) says they ran v1 in production for a month and found it "solid, but review every generated migration." I only saw it in search results and didn't open it, so treat it as a lead rather than confirmation. I only found the three headline breaking changes listed above. I didn't find a full list of smaller ones, so read the migration guide on that page before you upgrade.

Your research vault had nothing on Drizzle. I saved these sources and added a new page, `wiki/Drizzle ORM v1.md`, to the vault index. The vault's lint check found no problems.

Coverage: docs and GitHub issues via Exa search, with the three primary pages opened. Social: last30days wasn't run, so I have no reports from practitioners beyond the one blog post above. Tavily and Firecrawl weren't used. No paid spend.

graders.evidence:
**Yes, with one big caveat.** Drizzle ORM v1.0 went stable on 2026-09-15, and running it in production is reasonable on **1.0.3 or later**. But one bug that can lose data is still open: **if you change an enum, read the generated migration line by line before you apply it.** Details are saved in the vault at `wiki/Drizzle ORM v1.md`.

### What breaks when you upgrade
From the official upgrade guide ([orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1), 2026-09-15):

1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** Any code that uses `db.query.*` may return differently shaped results. Check every place you rely on nested relations.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is now `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update your package scripts, CI steps and docs.
3. **Postgres drivers have new minimums:** node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+. Bump the driver before or together with Drizzle.

### Known bugs to watch
- **#5120: still open as of today, 61 comments** ([issue](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5120), opened 2026-10-03). When you change an enum, the generated migration drops the column and recreates it instead of changing the enum in place, so the data in that column is lost. The only fix for now is to edit those migrations by hand.
- **#5188: fixed in 1.0.3** (2026-10-29, [issue](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5188)). On 1.0.0 to 1.0.2, the new relational queries returned wrongly nested results for tables that relate to themselves. Don't upgrade to anything below 1.0.3.

### How solid the evidence is
- I found only one first-hand production report: a team blog from 2026-10-18 ([link](https://blog.example-dev.io/drizzle-v1-in-production)) that ran v1 for a month and found it "solid, but review every generated migration." It's a single anecdote, but it points at the same risk as #5120.

- The official guide says it includes a step-by-step migration section, but the page text I retrieved only had the summary list above. Read the full page before you upgrade in case it covers more.

**Suggested upgrade order:** bump the Postgres driver → upgrade to `drizzle-orm` 1.0.3+ → rename `push` to `sync` in scripts and CI → test your relational queries → read every generated migration before applying it, especially any that touch enums.
